title: NUMA-aware worker placement and syscall coalescing probe
body:
Goal:
Short probe to determine whether NUMA-affinity + syscall coalescing (eventfd/timerfd batching) buys tail-latency for tiny requests (~<150 tokens) in our production-like workload. We want a minimally invasive strategy we could ship as an opt-in runtime flag before pursuing deeper tokenizer/C-extension work.

Background / motivation:
- Many tail spikes we see correlate with worker wakeups across sockets and repeated epoll->read syscalls when a batch finishes.
- Prior notes focused on parser/tokenizer CPU cost; this probe looks at the infrastructure layer: placement of workers on NUMA nodes and reducing syscalls/wakeups that amplify latency variance.

Hypotheses:
1) Pinning request-processing workers and tokenizer helpers to the same NUMA node as the GPU driver/allocations reduces cross-node memory latency and page migration, lowering 95/99p by ~5-15%.
2) Coalescing small syscalls (grouping eventfd signals, batching timer expirations) reduces context switches and epoll wakeup fanout, improving median and tails for very small requests.

Testbed:
- c6g-like CPU machines (dual-socket), Linux 6.1 kernel, 128GB, same kernel boot flags as staging (transparent hugepages enabled), GLIBC 2.35.
- Serving binary: runtime:main@commit 9c1f2 (cpu-only build with tokenizer Python shim).
- Workload: synthetic small-requests generator mimicking prod: 10k rps, uniform 8-120 token sizes, client p99 think-time = 0ms to stress tails.
- Measurements: per-request latency histograms, perf (cycles, context-switches), pidstat, numastat, and flamegraph samples.

Experiments run:
A) Baseline: default Linux scheduler, workers not pinned. B) Pin workers (all IO and tokenizer pools) to socket 0 cpuset (numactl --physcpubind). C) Baseline + syscall coalescing shim (microqueue in runtime: accumulate up to N signals / 1ms before eventfd notify). D) Pin workers + coalescing shim.
Each run lasted 10 minutes and repeated 3x.

Key results (aggregate):
- Baseline: p50=6.8ms, p95=28.4ms, p99=73.1ms, ctx-switches per sec ~4.6k
- Pin only: p50=6.6ms, p95=23.7ms (-16%), p99=65.9ms (-10%), ctx-switches ~3.9k (-15%)
- Coalesce only: p50=6.4ms (-6%), p95=21.9ms (-23%), p99=58.2ms (-20%), ctx-switches ~2.8k (-40%)
- Pin + coalesce: p50=6.2ms, p95=19.8ms (-30%), p99=50.3ms (-31%), ctx-switches ~2.6k

Observations / signals:
- numastat shows ~30% fewer remote node allocations in pin runs. Page fault rates dropped during bursts when tokenizer scratch buffers were reused.
- Perf sampling indicates fewer user→kernel transitions with coalescing shim; many epoll_wait wakeups were collapsed into single handler runs.
- Coalescing increases latency variance slightly at very low load (some requests wait up to N ms intentionally), but at target load (10k rps) tradeoff is positive: reduced tail from fewer context switches and less cross-core handoff.
- Noticed a side-effect: when coalescing is enabled, debug logging that flushes synchronously can cause a batch to hold notifications longer; we need to ensure flushes are async or bounded.

Risks / caveats:
- Busy-waiting vs coalescing: cannot spin to avoid syscalls (costly on shared machines). We used eventfd with short deadline (1ms) to bound additional latency; tuning needed per instance class.
- NUMA pinning reduces scheduler flexibility; on multi-tenant hosts this may be counterproductive unless enforced via cgroups / dedicated capacity.
- Interaction with Python GIL: pinned tokenizer helpers are still Python threads in many cases; reducing cross-socket memory helps but GIL contention remains. This is an operational improvement, not a substitute for tokenizer C-extension.

Recommendations / next steps:
1) Feature flag: add runtime flag --numa-worker-affinity with mode {off,prefer-local,hard-pin} and --eventfd-coalesce-ms=<int>. Default off.
2) Short-term rollout path: enable in dedicated GPU pools where we control tenancy and NUMA topology. Run canary with --eventfd-coalesce-ms=1 and monitoring for p95/p99 and cpu steal.
3) Instrumentation: add counters for coalesced-notifications, average coalesce delay, and separate latency histograms for coalesced vs immediate deliveries.
4) Fixes: make all logging flush async/queued when coalescing enabled. Ensure tokenization scratch buffer pre-touching to reduce page faults on first use.
5) Longer term: consider tokenizer C-extension + preallocated per-NUMA memory pools to further cut p99. Explore integrating coalescing logic with batching decisions (e.g., allow N-ms coalesce only when batch-length < X).

Open questions:
- Optimal coalesce window: 1ms worked well on these machines, but how does it interact with high-IO instances? Need matrix across instance classes.
- How to safely expose NUMA pinning in hosted environments? Likely only for Dedicated.
- Can we adaptively coalesce (signal-rate-based) rather than static timeout?

Action items:
- [Ariella] prototype runtime flags + metrics (2 wks).
- [Jonah] add canary config for dedicated pools, include numactl and cpuset validation (1 wk).
- [Maya] run extended soak across instance families and collect telemetry (2 wks).

Appendix (quick notes from perf samples):
- In baseline hot paths, top kernel symbols: epoll_wait, futex_wait, schedule. With coalescing these drop ~30% in stack samples and scheduler/syscall overhead moves proportionally to user-level compute.
- Command lines used for pinning: taskset -c 0-15 /srv/runtime ... and systemd CPUAffinity in prod units for hard-pin tests.

If this looks promising we can wrap the coalescing logic behind an adaptive controller that monitors wakeup rate and dynamically tunes the window. For now the minimal flagged rollout in Dedicated will give strong signal.
